pr_comments: Passing

Thinking about this more, I can think of four different ways that applications do shutdown for TLS at the moment. We should consider how we handle each of these in QUIC and ensure that what we've got in the PR meets all of them, or at least we understand what the differences in behaviour are and have documented them.

1) Abrupt shutdown: In this case the application doesn't call SSL_shutdown() at all. It just stops calling SSL_read()/SSL_write() once its finished reading/sending the data it wants and calls SSL_free(). No close_notify gets sent.

2) Single sided shutdown: The application just calls SSL_shutdown() once to send a close_notify and then immediately calls SSL_free().

3) Two sided shutdown: The application keeps calling SSL_shutdown() until it gets a return value of 1

4) Two sided shutdown with read: The application calls SSL_shutdown() once and then calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated.

More TLS application scenarios:

5. Remote initiated two-sided shutdown: The applications calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated, then the application then calls SSL_shutdown()

6. Remote initiated one-sided shutdown: The application calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated and then just calls SSL_free()

7. Remote initiated abrupt shutdown: The peer just closes the TCP connection abruptly. Calls to SSL_read() return SSL_ERROR_SSL (or SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN if SSL_OP_IGNORE_UNEXPECTED_EOF is set).

>1) Abrupt shutdown: In this case the application doesn't call SSL_shutdown() at all. It just stops calling SSL_read()/SSL_write() once its finished reading/sending the data it wants and calls SSL_free(). No close_notify gets sent.

Of course this is currently OK.

>2) Single sided shutdown: The application just calls SSL_shutdown() once to send a close_notify and then immediately calls SSL_free().

This corresponds to rapid shutdown mode here; the application calls SSL_shutdown_ex with `SSL_SHUTDOWN_FLAG_RAPID`, meaning we do not go through the RFC-compliant post-closure wait periods (equivalent to TCP `CLOSE_WAIT`/`TIME_WAIT`. So the application can do this if it wants.

>3) Two sided shutdown: The application keeps calling SSL_shutdown() until it gets a return value of 1

This is our normal behaviour for SSL_shutdown with QUIC.

>4) Two sided shutdown with read: The application calls SSL_shutdown() once and then calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated.

I don't think this can be made compatible with the semantics of QUIC. Once we send CONNECTION_CLOSE everything is dead — it's not like TLS over TCP where `close_notify` seems to be more of a polite request and things can be temporarily half-open in the return direction.

Our only option would be to not send CONNECTION_CLOSE immediately when SSL_shutdown is called. But that doesn't work either because we then don't know when the peer has stopped sending application data and that it's safe to send CONNECTION_CLOSE.

Indeed it's actually called "Immediate Close" in the RFC, touching on this fact. I suspect where application protocols need a more orchestrated shutdown process this will be managed via application-layer protocol messages.

>5. Remote initiated two-sided shutdown: The applications calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated, then the application then calls SSL_shutdown()

So here the `SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN` implies the end of the stream, not the connection. So this would actually be a locally initiated shutdown. Obviously another possibility is remote connection termination in which case we enter the `TERMINATING`/`TERMINATED` states and SSL_shutdown is a no-op.

>6. Remote initiated one-sided shutdown: The application calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated and then just calls SSL_free()

Works.

>7. Remote initiated abrupt shutdown: The peer just closes the TCP connection abruptly. Calls to SSL_read() return SSL_ERROR_SSL (or SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN if SSL_OP_IGNORE_UNEXPECTED_EOF is set).

Doesn't seem to be relevant here

>> Abrupt shutdown: In this case the application doesn't call SSL_shutdown() at all. It just stops calling SSL_read()/SSL_write() once its finished reading/sending the data it wants and calls SSL_free(). No close_notify gets sent.
> Of course this is currently OK.

Although its not quite the same. In a TLS app if you call SSL_write() and get a success response and then call SSL_free() then the data has been sent. I think the kernel will ensure that any buffered data is sent? With our QUIC implementation if you call SSL_free() any buffered data is lost. Probably there is not much we can do about this other than document it. Essentially with TLS you can get away without doing a graceful shutdown and it may work anyway. With QUIC you really have to do the shutdown.

>> Single sided shutdown: The application just calls SSL_shutdown() once to send a close_notify and then immediately calls SSL_free().
>
> This corresponds to rapid shutdown mode here; the application calls SSL_shutdown_ex with SSL_SHUTDOWN_FLAG_RAPID, meaning we do not go through the RFC-compliant post-closure wait periods (equivalent to TCP CLOSE_WAIT/TIME_WAIT. So the application can do this if it wants.

So, if the application calls the old SSL_shutdown() (i.e. not SSL_shutdown_ex) and then immediately calls SSL_free() this is effectively the same right? This is presumably not a recommended approach but it will work in a similar way to TLS.

>> Two sided shutdown with read: The application calls SSL_shutdown() once and then calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated.
>
> I don't think this can be made compatible with the semantics of QUIC. Once we send CONNECTION_CLOSE everything is dead — it's not like TLS over TCP where close_notify seems to be more of a polite request and things can be temporarily half-open in the return direction.
>
> Our only option would be to not send CONNECTION_CLOSE immediately when SSL_shutdown is called. But that doesn't work either because we then don't know when the peer has stopped sending application data and that it's safe to send CONNECTION_CLOSE.
>
> Indeed it's actually called "Immediate Close" in the RFC, touching on this fact. I suspect where application protocols need a more orchestrated shutdown process this will be managed via application-layer protocol messages.

As mentioned above we *could* allow continued SSL_read() calls on already buffered data. Or alternatively maybe its an error if there is buffered data to be read when attempting to shutdown? It seems odd that otherwise that data is just silently discarded and everything is apparently "successful".

Ultimately though it comes back to the altered semantics of SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN which no longer indicates a closed connection: it indicates a closed stream.

I think there does need to be some discussion about this difference between TLS and QUIC in the SSL_shutdown docs. If you write a TLS application that works this way then you will end up with a fully standards compliant two-sided shutdown. But with QUIC the only way to get the fully standards compliant behaviour is to call SSL_shutdown() twice.

>> Remote initiated two-sided shutdown: The applications calls SSL_read() until SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is indicated, then the application then calls SSL_shutdown()
>
> So here the SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN implies the end of the stream, not the connection. So this would actually be a locally initiated shutdown. Obviously another possibility is remote connection termination in which case we enter the TERMINATING/TERMINATED states and SSL_shutdown is a no-op.

So in this case what happens in the event that we attempt a read on a stream but the peer has closed the connection? Do we get SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN or SSL_ERROR_SSL?

> Although its not quite the same. In a TLS app if you call SSL_write() and get a success response and then call SSL_free() then the data has been sent. I think the kernel will ensure that any buffered data is sent? With our QUIC implementation if you call SSL_free() any buffered data is lost. Probably there is not much we can do about this other than document it. Essentially with TLS you can get away without doing a graceful shutdown and it may work anyway. With QUIC you really have to do the shutdown.

Hm... this makes me wonder if we should have an API that would inform you when all data from a stream was acked by peer. IMO not necessarily for MVP but something that we might need to have.

However in the TLS case it is not that much different - although SSL_write() ensures the data is sent it does not ensure that it was received by the other side. So IMO just documenting the difference would be fine at least for MVP.

>So, if the application calls the old SSL_shutdown() (i.e. not SSL_shutdown_ex) and then immediately calls SSL_free() this is effectively the same right? This is presumably not a recommended approach but it will work in a similar way to TLS.

SSL_shutdown is the same as SSL_shutdown_ex with no flags. If you don't specify `RAPID` it will wait for the post-termination wait process as specified in the RFC. So everything should work OK.

>As mentioned above we could allow continued SSL_read() calls on already buffered data. Or alternatively maybe its an error if there is buffered data to be read when attempting to shutdown? It seems odd that otherwise that data is just silently discarded and everything is apparently "successful".

If an application hasn't called SSL_read() before shutting down presumably it isn't interested in it.

It is worth noting that while a kernel will try to ensure delivery of data after closing a TCP socket, this is no guarantee it made it to the peer application. Even if a TCP ACK is received from the peer, this is generated automatically by the peer kernel and doesn't indicate the data made it to the peer application. The general principle is that application layer receipt of some piece of information requires application layer acknowledgement.

>Ultimately though it comes back to the altered semantics of SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN which no longer indicates a closed connection: it indicates a closed stream.
>
>I think there does need to be some discussion about this difference between TLS and QUIC in the SSL_shutdown docs. If you write a TLS application that works this way then you will end up with a fully standards compliant two-sided shutdown. But with QUIC the only way to get the fully standards compliant behaviour is to call SSL_shutdown() twice.

Hmm? In blocking mode you only need to call SSL_shutdown() once.

In non-blocking mode with rapid mode and no stream flush flags you could only call it once. There is a risk of the CONNECTION_CLOSE frame which is sent being lost in this case. But if the caller doesn't want to hang around before calling `SSL_free` this is unavoidable.
The docs for the QUIC-specific aspects of SSL_shutdown were added to the manpage some time ago; feedback on that section would be welcomed

> If an application hasn't called SSL_read() before shutting down presumably it isn't interested in it.

Well not necessarily. At least in TLS this half-close is perfectly normal. But thinking about it I suppose this is a fundamental difference between TLS and QUIC and we shouldn't try to replicate this TLS behaviour in QUIC.

But this leads me to another thought. Is leaving unread data in the buffers on shutdown a success condition? I'm thinking of the equivalent with TCP sockets...if you "close" a TCP socket which has data available to read that you haven't consumed then a TCP RST is sent rather than closing the socket normally. Having data left over that you haven't read suggests some kind of application protocol error to me. The application may not even be aware that there *is* data to be read - so then you have the situation where one endpoint has failed to process all the data because of some problem and closes thinking it is completing normally. The other endpoint may also believe that all the data it sent was processed successfully.

You could easily argue that the onus here is on the application to always check that all the data in all its streams was fully consumed - but I'm wondering if that is the best approach. It seems like a lot of applications would need to do that and something that a lot would get wrong.

> Hmm? In blocking mode you only need to call SSL_shutdown() once.

Right - yeah sorry. I was mainly thinking of the non-blocking case (and then I suppose I should have said you have to call SSL_shutdown at least twice).

I've created a ticket for us to separately review and update the SSL_shutdown docs in light of the discussion above.

The only question I still have about this PR is whether shutting down with unread data in the read buffers should be a success condition or not as per my comment above.

The TCP behaviour you mention is interesting. I actually wasn't aware of this.

Still, if we call `SSL_shutdown` and have data available to be read, how would we go about informing the remote party? QUIC doesn't really make much of a distinction between normal and abnormal connection termination, unlike TCP. It is possible we could promote an application CONNECTION_CLOSE structure to a transport CONNECTION_CLOSE structure if there is unread data, but that just seems likely to annoy applications which don't need the unread data because they have agreed to close the connection immediately at the application level.

My feeling here is that because QUIC streams have their own FIN signalling, an application which wants to know that all data sent on a stream has been received can do that via the per-stream signalling. But I'm open to other ideas.

It occurs to me that this situation could actually occur in TLS, i.e. we have read a TLS record, decrypted and buffered it. It may have been partially read by the application but with data remaining in our buffers. If the application then calls SSL_shutdown() without reading it, I think we just discard it. It would seem strange to do something different with QUIC, so I think I've convinced myself that this isn't a problem.

> If the application then calls SSL_shutdown() without reading it, I think we just discard it.

....except we don't. We'll never read a close_notify from the peer if we've got buffered app data waiting to be read.

In any case I'm still ok with my approval here. QUIC is just different in this regards.

24 hours has passed since 'approval: done' was set, but as this PR has been updated in that time the label 'approval: ready to merge' is not being automatically set.  Please review the updates and set the label manually.

> Hm... this makes me wonder if we should have an API that would inform you when all data from a stream was acked by peer. IMO not necessarily for MVP but something that we might need to have.
> 
> However in the TLS case it is not that much different - although SSL_write() ensures the data is sent it does not ensure that it was received by the other side. So IMO just documenting the difference would be fine at least for MVP.

With TLS, an application can confirm that the application on the other side has processed all the data using an application protocol message or use the close notify (with SSL_shutdown() or SSL_read() with SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN). I expect this functionality to be available in the first release with QUIC.

I think the normal expectation is that SSL_shutdown() will only confirm the closure when all data has been acked.

> With TLS, an application can confirm that the application on the other side has processed all the data using an application protocol message or use the close notify (with SSL_shutdown() or SSL_read() with SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN). I expect this functionality to be available in the first release with QUIC.
>
> I think the normal expectation is that SSL_shutdown() will only confirm the closure when all data has been acked.

This is the functionality which this PR provides. When you call `SSL_shutdown` any streams are drained and we wait until the peer finishes ACKing all sent data. So there is reliable transmission here.

SSL_shutdown closes an entire connection. You can finish an individual stream using SSL_stream_conclude which concludes the sending part of a QUIC stream; this is how QUIC works and the closest analogue is TCP half-closure. Likewise when reading from the read part of a stream, EOF is indicated using SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN in the normal manner. In other words, SSL_ERROR_ZERO_RETURN is now a piece of information on stream state, not connection state.

issue_context.title: No way to do a graceful shutdown with QUIC
issue_context.body:
The semantics of SSL_shutdown() seem to be fundamentally different in QUIC compared to TLS.

In TLS SSL_shutdown() is a *graceful* shutdown. Any existing data left to be sent is still sent and you can continue to read data until the peer also indicates shutdown.

IIUC, in QUIC SSL_shutdown() causes a connection close to be sent which is *immediate*. Any unacked data that we've sent is potentially lost and we cannot continue to read data from the peer.

In fact there does not currently seem to be a way to do graceful shutdown with our APIs as they currently stand, e.g. how can an application know that all data it has sent has actually been received before it decides to close down the connection?

review_comments: IIUC at this point all our send streams have been flushed and we can no longer write any more data.  If there was no data to flush then we immediately proceed to connection closure without ever returning 0 in between. I'm not sure this is correct - or at least its not obviously correct. In TLS you can call SSL_shutdown(), receive a 0 return (as long as the peer didn't already initiate shutdown) and then continue to call SSL_read() until the peer sends close_notify. This doesn't look like it will work here because we proceed to immediate closure.

Yeah here the shutdown is bidirectional where in TLS it is unidirectional. Now the question is whether unidirectional shutdown makes much sense in QUIC with streams and SSL_stream_conclude(), I doubt it.

I guess here you're basically describing TCP-like half-closure semantics.

I'm not sure how this would work with QUIC as there's no equivalent half-closure state. Once we send CONNECTION_CLOSE that's it. We can continue to allow SSL_read of course for any residual data, but as per the RFC we can't really receive any new data from the peer.
I think its the continued ability to allow SSL_read() that I'm mostly concerned about (e.g. to receive already buffered data) then that is probably close enough??
Shouldn't we be marking all streams with FIN during this flush?
Why? The streams weren't concluded by the application, IMO it would be incorrect.

Well they were implicitly concluded by virtue of initiating a graceful shutdown which prevents further writes on those streams. Obviously you wouldn't do this in the SSL_SHUTDOWN_FLAG_NO_STREAM_FLUSH case which is more of a non-graceful shutdown of the streams.

This is a deliberate decision, and basically why I changed my mind.

By basic reasoning here is that a stream being FIN'd has application semantics. There's potentially a semantic difference between an application receiving data on a stream and then the connection is shutdown, and that stream being FIN'd and then the connection is shutdown.

In fact some application protocols forbid some streams ever be closed and treat such an event as an application-level protocol violation. So this would preclude use of shutdown flush with those stream types.
How do we test blocking SSL_shutdown then?

Currently we can't. Actually this is a large blind spot in our testing right now — at some point I want the multistream test to be runnable in blocking mode. Probably will need to spin up a thread to tick the TSERVER and only support this test in builds with threads.
